title: Little confidence IAG will get RAC over line, despite promises
full_text:
The market does not think IAG will get its proposed purchase of RAC Insurance over the line with the competition watchdog, despite the listed insurer desperately promising to offload its West Australian NRMA loan book.
The $19.4bn IAG, in its public benefits application following the ACCC opposing the acquisition, said it would sell the renewal rights of its home and motor book for WA NRMA, expand RAC policy insurance in WA’s remote north, invest money in the local community and even offered “stronger measures” should IAG breach “particular requirements”. IAG did not provide much detail about the said measures.
Despite all this grovelling, market watchers still aren’t hot on IAG’s chances of the $1.35bn deal proceeding much further.
In a note sent to clients after IAG’s announcement, Jarden analysts led by Blake Dowsett poured cold water on the deal.
“Whilst the structural nature of the renewal rights remedy should improve the probability of successful completion, our base case assumes the deal is ultimately not approved,” they wrote.
“We highlight that the ACCC has demonstrated a clear preference for structural remedies over behavioural, and hence we think the proposed sale of the existing NRMA book is likely to be positively received.
“While IAG has indicated it will increase the availability of home insurance, we expect the ACCC to focus on other factors such as pricing/T&Cs given insurance penetration is ultimately what drives the public benefit. The other measures offered are considered positive, but unlikely to significantly influence the ACCC decision.” The analysts point to pro-forma market share in Western Australia remaining high for the combined business, even with the NRMA sale. Estimates placed it between 50 per cent to 60 per cent market share in home insurance, and 55 to 56 per cent for motor.
The shape of the deal, struck in March, would see IAG pay the Royal Automobile Club of WA $400m for the RAC Insurance business and $950m for a 20-year licensing agreement so it can trade under the RAC banner.
After first indicating it expected $1.5bn in gross written premiums from the deal, IAG revised that number down to $1.2bn should it offload the NRMA renewal book.
IAG boss Nick Hawkins promised RAC customers a healthy future for the business. “RAC is a wonderful organisation with a much-loved brand,” he said. “We are committed to creating this strategic alliance and are making substantial commitments to RAC, its members and all Western Australians.”
